column2: The Lord speaks to Moses; the saying formula introduces the following instructions. No second speaker or additional audience is inferred before the next verse names Israel.

The condition concerns an individual who unintentionally violates one of the Lord's prohibitions. Soul is a personal designation; unintentionally qualifies the sin, and the forbidden acts are not turned into commands to perform them.

The anointed high priest's sin is linked to the people's sinning by an articular infinitive. Retain the resulting involvement provisionally, the unblemished calf and both repeated references to his sin.
column3: Precise purpose/result relation between the high priest's act and the people's sinning.

column2: The calf is brought to the tent door; a singular hand is laid on its head and a singular actor slaughters it. All three appearances of being before the Lord remain, without smoothing away the repeated setting.

The anointed priest is additionally described with the consecrated-hands idiom. Some of the blood is English realization of the partitive construction. His consecration is not silently reduced to ordinary physical hand-washing.
column3: Full lexical review of the consecration idiom and its relation to the anointed-priest title.

column2: The priest dips a finger and sprinkles blood seven times before the Lord toward the holy veil. Direction toward the veil is preserved without asserting that each drop must strike its fabric.

Blood is placed on the incense-altar horns and poured at the whole-burnt-offering altar's base. Preserve both altars and their different locations; all the blood is read in the ritual sequence after the preceding applications.

The calf's fat is removed, followed by the explicit descriptions of fat covering and lying upon the inward parts. Sin offering renders the ritual use of sin, not a claim that the animal itself committed wrongdoing.

Two kidneys, their associated fat by the thighs and the liver lobe remain separate listed items. The removal parenthesis links the lobe with the kidneys. No modern anatomical identification beyond the inherited terms is asserted.
column3: Ancient anatomical identification of the lobe and surrounding fat.

column2: The fat-removal procedure is compared with the calf of the deliverance sacrifice, and the priest offers it on the offering altar. The selected altar noun is retained rather than automatically expanded to a longer familiar title.

Hide, all flesh, head, extremities, belly and dung form a continuing object list. The sentence continues into the carrying and burning instructions; the list does not itself introduce another offering category.

Plural agents carry the whole calf outside the camp to the clean ash-disposal place and burn it on wood. The final passive repeats the ash location. Do not insert a named actor where the source leaves the plural subject implicit.

Unintentional ignorance belongs to the whole congregation, followed by a matter escaping its eyes and the commission of a forbidden act. The collective-to-plural grammatical movement is retained; ignorance does not remove the stated offence.

The sin becomes known to the congregation, which then brings an unblemished calf to the tent doors. Preserve recognition as a separate development; the passive does not identify who disclosed the sin.

The congregation's elders lay their hands on the calf's head, and the slaughtering verb is also plural. Preserve both plural forms and the repeated before-the-Lord setting, without substituting a single representative priest.

The anointed priest brings some of the calf's blood into the Tent of Testimony. Here the direction is explicitly into; the separate identification of this priest is retained rather than absorbed into the elders of the preceding verse.

The finger-and-blood action precedes seven sprinklings before the Lord in front of the holy veil. Seven and the veil's holiness remain explicit. The concise inherited English supplies the understood blood object of sprinkling.

The compounded-incense altar is identified as before the Lord and within the tent; all blood is then poured at the offering altar's base by the door. Preserve both descriptive clauses and the change of altar.
All fat is removed and offered on the altar. The singular actor continues the priestly procedure; no new animal, amount or additional location is supplied to this short instruction.

The calf is treated like the earlier sin-offering calf. The passive thus it shall be done repeats that conformity, while the priest's atonement and the passive forgiveness of their sin remain separate clauses.

Plural actors carry the whole calf out and burn it like the former calf. The concluding designation identifies this as the congregation's sin offering. The comparison is to the prior ritual, not to an independently invented sacrifice.
The ruler unintentionally performs a forbidden act, sins and incurs offence. Their God is plural in the Greek possessive and is retained; it is not normalized to the ruler's singular his God.

When the ruler's sin becomes known, his gift is an unblemished male young goat. The sex and condition are explicit and distinguish this offering from the female goat permitted later for an individual.

A singular hand is laid on the goat's head, but the slaughtering verb is plural. The location is where whole burnt offerings are slaughtered before the Lord. Retain the number shift and sin-offering designation.

The priest applies some blood with a finger to the whole-burnt-offering altar's horns, then pours all its blood beside that altar's base. The altar title is repeated in the source and remains repeated in English.

All fat is offered like that of the deliverance sacrifice. Atonement for the ruler from his sin precedes passive forgiveness. The inherited from-phrase remains provisional; forgiveness is not rewritten as the priest's explicit direct act.
column3: Precise force of the from-sin construction with the atonement verb.

column2: One person from the people of the land unintentionally violates a prohibition and incurs offence. Preserve the individual's ordinary-community setting and the stated unintentional character rather than transferring the ruler's status into this case.

The known sin calls for an unblemished female young goat. The bringing verb is repeated before the reference to the sin committed; the inherited English retains that repetition and the contrast with the male ruler's goat.

The offerer lays one hand on the sin offering's head; plural agents slaughter the female goat where whole burnt offerings are slaughtered. Ritual sin-language is realized as offering language, and the female animal remains explicit.

A priest takes some blood with his finger, applies it to the altar horns and pours all the blood beside the base. The final shorter altar reference is retained; a second full title is not inserted merely for uniformity.

Fat removal parallels the deliverance sacrifice, followed here by an explicit sweet-aroma formula. Preserve that formula where present, then the priest's atonement and passive forgiveness, rather than making every parallel paragraph identical.

This alternative follows the preceding female-goat case and specifies an unblemished female sheep. The sheep rendering is contextually appropriate here; the broader flock-animal rendering elsewhere is not imposed mechanically on every occurrence.

A singular hand is laid on the offering's head, followed by plural slaughtering at the whole-burnt-offering location. The source does not repeat the animal's sex or species in this unit, so the pronoun remains.

The priest takes and applies blood with a finger, then pours all blood at the base. The selected noun here is whole burning; the inherited wording preserves its distinction from the plural whole burnt offerings elsewhere.

Sheep fat is removed as in the deliverance sacrifice and placed on the altar upon the Lord's whole burnt offering. The final atonement-for-the-committed-sin and forgiveness clauses complete this case without adding an explicit new agent of forgiveness.

The person hears an adjuration and is a witness through sight or knowledge, but fails to report. The conditional relationships are retained: hearing an adjuration by itself is not translated as the offence. Bearing the sin remains the stated consequence.

The long list distinguishes an unclean thing, a dead thing, prey torn by beasts and additional dead/unclean categories, ending with livestock carcasses. Preserve the repetition and continuing sentence rather than replacing it with a shorter familiar list.

Human uncleanness adds another contact case. The condition includes an initial failure to notice, later knowledge and guilt. Keep that sequence without treating ritual defilement as a modern medical diagnosis.

The oath expressly concerns doing evil or good, with lip-declaration, subsequent unawareness and recognition. Rashness is not inserted as a separate Greek adjective. The eye phrase is realized by escapes his notice, with the literal image available in the close draft.

Confession concerns the sin and the matters in which the person sinned. Retain the inherited concise formulation provisionally; the final against-it pronoun is difficult and is not assigned a new explicit referent.
column3: Force and antecedent of the final kat autes phrase; full construction accounting remains open.

column2: A female flock animal is specified as a ewe lamb or female young goat. Both permitted categories and the repeated sin clauses remain, followed by priestly atonement and passive forgiveness. The offering is not restricted to sheep alone.

The hand idiom expresses insufficient means. Propose animal from the flock instead of sheep because the preceding eligible offering explicitly includes a female goat. The two birds remain alternatives, with one for sin and one for whole burning.

The priest presents the bird for sin first and handles its head at the neck joint without dividing it. Preserve priority, agent and negative restriction; the precise removal technique cannot be settled from an English label alone.
column3: Exact ritual force of the head/vertebra construction and prohibition on dividing.

column2: Some blood is sprinkled on the altar wall while the remainder is drained at its base. The two locations and actions remain distinct. The final for-sin explanation identifies the ritual category rather than a second bird.

The second bird is prepared as a whole burnt offering as is fitting. Priest, atonement for the committed sin and passive forgiveness remain. The source's general conformity expression is not expanded into an invented procedural quotation.

The further inability case permits a tenth of an oiphi of fine flour. Neither oil nor frankincense is added because this is for sin. Keep the ancient measure and both prohibitions without a guessed modern conversion.
column3: Historical capacity of the oiphi and the ritual classification require specialist review.

column2: The priest explicitly takes a full handful and places its memorial portion on the whole-burnt-offering altar. This verse names the taking agent; it does not by itself settle every less explicit participial construction in chapter 2.

Atonement and forgiveness apply to any one of the stated cases. The remainder belongs to the priest as with the fine-flour sacrifice. Keep the comparison and the distinction between the memorial portion and what remains.

The Lord's speaking to Moses introduces a new set of conditions. Preserve this fresh speech formula rather than treating the following holy-things case as merely another ingredient option for the preceding offering.

Forgetfulness and unintentional sin concern the Lord's holy things. The offering is an unblemished ram valued in silver shekels by the sanctuary standard; no specific number of shekels is supplied by this wording.
column3: Valuation construction and the scope of offences against holy things.

column2: Restitution for the holy things is increased by a fifth and paid to the priest. Atonement with the guilt-offering ram and forgiveness follow. The surcharge is additional to the principal; the verse does not replace restitution with the animal alone.

A person commits a forbidden act without knowing it, incurs guilt and bears the sin. Unawareness and responsibility are both explicit. The wording is retained without resolving the legal category by a modern rule about intent.

An unblemished silver-valued ram is brought to the priest. The repeated ignorance language and the separate statement that the person did not know remain, followed by forgiveness; neither clause is removed as redundant.

The cognate offence verb and noun intensify the statement before the Lord. Indeed is a provisional English realization of that emphasis; it is not an extra assertion added merely to create an elevated style.

A fresh divine speech formula introduces the property and false-oath cases. Preserve the boundary even though these verses are placed in another chapter in some numbering systems; the selected source keeps them in chapter 5.

The doubled disregard construction supplies the emphasis in utterly disregards. Deposit, partnership, robbery and another wrong to a neighbour remain separate cases. The ancient legal relation called partnership requires fuller lexical assessment.
column3: Precise scope of koinonia in this property-law context.

column2: Finding lost property, dealing falsely about it and swearing unjustly extend the preceding cases. Preserve the general any-of-all wording and the link to sin; this is not an unrelated prohibition of every oath regardless of context.

The restitution list repeats seized goods, wrongfully obtained property, an entrusted deposit and a found lost item. The legal condition continues into the principal-and-fifth payment; its clause sequence remains provisional rather than reordered as a new legal system.
column3: Relationship of the return clause to the conditional sequence and subsequent repayment.

column2: The principal and an additional fifth are restored to the owner on the day the offender is convicted or exposed. Preserve that temporal marker rather than substitute the day of the offence or a freely chosen offering date.
column3: Exact juridical force of the passive verb rendered convicted.

column2: The offender brings an unblemished ram with a valuation related to the offence. The final to/against-him pronoun is retained in the inherited divine-reference reading provisionally; the source itself does not encode English devotional capitalization.
column3: Referent of the final pronoun and its relation to the valuation/offence phrase.

column2: The priest makes atonement before the Lord and forgiveness concerns any of the committed offences. Keep the comprehensive wording and the final pronoun while leaving its referent subject to the same review as verse 25.
column3: Referent of the final pronoun; capitalization is an editorial interpretation.

column2: The divine speech formula introduces instructions for Aaron and his sons. Preserve its place at the start of this source-numbered chapter rather than renumbering it to follow a different Bible tradition.

The burning-place clause covers the whole night until morning; remain supplies English support for the nominal construction. The altar fire burns and is not quenched. Preserve both the time span and the negative directive.

The priest wears a linen tunic and linen lower garment, removes the burnt material from the altar and places it beside the altar. Burnt remains is contextual and provisional; no modern combustion process is asserted.
column3: Precise ritual-material sense of the noun rendered burnt remains.

column2: The priest changes from his robe into another before carrying the burnt remains outside the camp to a clean place. Both garment actions and the external clean location remain, without a guessed explanation of the change.

The selected text says the altar fire burns from it, then orders morning wood, the whole burnt offering and deliverance-offering fat. Retain the difficult from-phrase rather than silently substitute on it; all actions and their order remain.
column3: Referent and force of the from-it phrase describing the fire.

column2: Continual burning and the prohibition on quenching are both explicit. This repetition is not deleted as redundant, and continually is warranted here by the source duration expression rather than added as devotional emphasis.

Aaron's sons bring the sacrifice before the Lord opposite the altar. The relative clause identifies the act governed by this law; the particular flour preparation is developed next without inserting a new title here.

A handful of flour with oil and the frankincense on the sacrifice forms the altar offering and memorial portion. The pleasant-aroma formula remains. English he continues the priestly action without claiming a new named subject.

Aaron and his sons eat the remainder unleavened in a holy place, specified as the tent court. The subject is compound even though the first Greek verb is singular; no exclusive consumption by Aaron alone is inferred.

The offering is not baked leavened; the speaker has assigned it as a portion from the Lord's offerings. Its most-holy status is compared with sin and guilt offerings. Preserve both comparisons and the divine first-person gift.

Every male among the priests may eat the portion, and the statute spans generations. The contact clause says the toucher shall be sanctified; it is not rewritten as a prior qualification already possessed by the toucher.
column3: Precise ritual effect and legal force of the sanctification-by-contact statement.

column2: A new Lord-to-Moses speech introduces the anointing-day gift. Preserve that boundary rather than merging it into the general priestly eating rules, since the subsequent priest's offering has a different consumption rule.

Aaron and his sons bring a tenth of an oiphi, divided equally between morning and evening. You anoint him is second-person singular addressing Moses; it is not changed to a passive or to divine-address Thou.

The preparation includes a griddle, oil, mixing, rolled pieces and fragments, with sacrifice repeated. Retain the difficult preparation vocabulary provisionally rather than replace it with a modern recipe inferred from another textual tradition.
column3: Exact form and preparation of the rolled pieces and fragments.

column2: The anointed successor priest from Aaron's sons prepares the offering. The closing verb states complete performance; it does not itself repeat the verb burn. Preserve that distinction while reading the explicit whole-burning rule in verse 16.

Every priest's sacrifice is wholly burned and is not eaten. The negative consumption rule remains explicit and is not harmonized with the remainder allotted to priests in the earlier general-offering paragraph.

The Lord speaks again to Moses before addressing Aaron and his sons about sin offerings. The speech marker preserves the transition between the priest's own offering and the following more general procedure.

The sin offerings are slaughtered where the whole burnt offering is slaughtered before the Lord. The selected Greek shifts from a singular whole-burnt-offering expression to plural sin-offering items; the candidate preserves that difference.

The priest who offers the sacrifice eats it in a holy place, namely the tent court. Keep the actor-specific allocation and location, subject to the later exception for offerings whose blood enters the sanctuary.

Touching the flesh brings sanctification, and blood-splashed clothing is washed in a holy place. The difficult relative construction is retained without claiming whether only the stained area or the entire garment must be washed.
column3: Scope of the blood-sprinkled garment reference and sanctification clause.

column2: An earthenware cooking vessel is broken; a bronze vessel is scoured and rinsed with water. The material-based contrast and both cleansing actions remain. No scientific explanation of the differing rules is inserted.

Every male among the priests eats the specified items, which are most holy to the Lord. The plural object and the Lord reference remain explicit; the permission is not widened to every person in a priestly household.

Sin offerings whose blood enters the tent for atonement in the holy place are excluded from eating and must be burned. Preserve the qualifying blood condition so the exception does not become a ban on eating every sin offering.
The selected heading expressly names the ram for the guilt offering and its most-holy status. Retain ram rather than shorten the heading to an abstract guilt category that omits the stated animal.

Plural agents slaughter the ram at the whole-burnt-offering location, then a singular agent pours blood around the altar base. The base is expressly named here; it is not replaced with another blood-placement formula.
column3: Implicit subject of the singular blood-pouring verb after plural slaughterers.

column2: All fat, the loin and fat covering and resting on the inward parts continue the object list. Preserve loin as the selected Greek anatomical term rather than automatically substitute the familiar fat-tail description.
column3: Precise anatomical extent of the loin and associated fat.

column2: The two kidneys, associated fat and liver lobe are listed, with a plural removal object in the parenthesis. The inherited these reflects that plural instead of silently making every parallel anatomical instruction singular.

The priest offers the listed portions on the altar as an offering to the Lord, with the concluding guilt designation retained. The ritual category is not merged with the deliverance sacrifice merely because some handling is similar.

Every male among the priests eats the portions in a holy place. The shift from a distributive individual to plural eaters is natural to the group; the most-holy formula remains without naming an unexpressed room.

The sin and guilt offerings share one stated law, and the portion belongs to the priest making atonement with it. Read this within the allocation context; it does not erase every procedural distinction between the two offerings.

The priest presenting a person's whole burnt offering receives its hide. The repeated offering relationship is retained so the allocation is tied to the officiating priest, not to any unexpressed group of priests.

Oven, hearth and griddle preparations belong to the priest presenting them. Preserve the three preparation settings and the repeated ownership statement. Exact ancient equipment identification remains provisional.
column3: Distinction between hearth/grill and griddle in the selected cooking terminology.

column2: Preparations with oil and those not so prepared are assigned equally to all Aaron's sons. Not so prepared avoids assuming that the negative necessarily means uncooked. Each an equal share reflects the explicit equality clause.
The law of the deliverance sacrifice introduces what they bring to the Lord. Keep this selected ritual label provisional and distinct from the guilt-offering material immediately preceding it.

The praise offering includes fine-flour loaves prepared with oil, unleavened coated wafers and flour mixed with oil. Unleavened modifies the wafers explicitly here; it is not inserted into the first loaf description from another tradition.

Leavened loaves accompany the gifts and the sacrifice of praise and deliverance. Preserve the explicit leavened category without asserting that these loaves are burned on the altar; the sentence concerns bringing them with the gift.

One from all the gifts is set apart to the Lord and belongs to the priest pouring the blood. The source's one/from-all construction is retained without deciding how many bread categories must each supply a portion.
column3: Whether one from all has a distributive force over the several kinds of gifts.

column2: The flesh belongs to him and is eaten on the day of giving, with none left until morning. The antecedent of him is retained without inserting priest or offerer; the exact relation to the allocated portion remains open.
column3: Antecedent of his and relation of the flesh allocation to the preceding priestly portion.

column2: A vow or voluntary sacrifice may be eaten on the day of presentation and the following day. Preserve the two categories and the extra day rather than carry over the praise offering's same-day restriction.
Flesh remaining until the third day is burned with fire. Third day and the material to be burned remain explicit; this rule does not authorize consumption until the end of that third day.

Eating on the third day makes the offering unacceptable and uncredited to the offerer, and the eater bears sin. The cognate eating construction adds emphasis but does not introduce a distinct second act of eating.

Flesh touching uncleanness is not eaten and is burned; a clean person may eat flesh. Preserve the distinction between contaminated food and the eater's condition, without converting this ritual paragraph into a general modern dietary claim.

The person eats the Lord's deliverance-sacrifice flesh while uncleanness remains upon him, and perishes from his people. Both the ownership and the person's condition remain; the wording does not name an enforcement mechanism.
column3: Precise sanction implied by perishing from the people in this legal setting.

column2: Contact with human, animal or other listed uncleanness is followed by eating the Lord's sacrificial flesh. Keep the combined condition and the sanction; the final consequence is not attached to contact alone by deleting the eating clause.
The renewed Lord-to-Moses speech introduces the fat and blood prohibitions. Preserve this boundary between the earlier consumption-time rules and the following material restrictions.

The prohibited fat is explicitly that of cattle, sheep and goats. All three animal categories remain; this sentence is not silently broadened to every conceivable species or narrowed to only one of the preceding sacrifices.

Fat from animals dead or torn by beasts may be used for work but not eaten as food. The permission/prohibition contrast remains. Neither a specific craft nor a medical rationale for the restriction is supplied.

Eating fat from the livestock used for the Lord's offerings carries the stated perishing sanction. Retain the qualifying animal category and the personal consequence without claiming a modern legal application.

The blood prohibition extends to every dwelling and expressly includes birds and livestock. The two animal categories and the geographical breadth remain; this does not erase the different blood-handling instructions for altar rituals.
Every person who eats blood is subject to the repeated perishing-from-the-people statement. The repeated soul designation marks the individual liable; an unexpressed human executor is not added.

A further divine speech introduces the portions brought and allocated from the deliverance sacrifice. Preserve the speech boundary rather than treating the following allocation as an exception to the blood prohibition.

The offerer brings a gift to the Lord from the deliverance sacrifice; both references to the Lord and the repeated sacrifice category remain. The verse does not specify a new sacrifice independent of the one being apportioned.

His hands bring the offerings, specifically fat upon the breast and the liver lobe, to place as a gift before the Lord. Preserve the liver item and presentation wording instead of importing a different wave-motion description.
The priest offers the fat on the altar, while the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons. Keep the different destinations; the entire breast is not described here as burned with its fat.

The right foreleg is set apart to the priest from the community's deliverance sacrifices. Foreleg reflects the Greek arm term; it is not replaced with thigh merely to agree with a familiar alternate textual base.
column3: Precise butchery designation of the arm/foreleg portion.

column2: Among Aaron's sons, the priest presenting the blood and fat receives the right foreleg as his portion. Preserve this actor-specific allocation and its distinction from the breast's broader priestly assignment.

The speaker has taken the presentation breast and set-apart foreleg from Israel's sacrifices and given them to Aaron and his sons. Your sacrifices is the selected second-person plural address; it is not normalized to their sacrifices.

Aaron's and his sons' anointing is linked to portions from the Lord's offerings and their priestly introduction. Retain anointing provisionally while recording a possible anointing-share sense; the implicit introducing actor is not newly named.
column3: Literal anointing versus the associated priestly share; subject of the introducing verb.

column2: The Lord's command concerns giving these portions from Israel on the day of anointing, with an enduring generational statute. Preserve the active he anointed them without asserting the implicit subject as certain.
column3: Implicit actor of anointing and attachment of the on-that-day phrase.

column2: Whole burnt offerings, sacrifice, sin, guilt, consecration and deliverance sacrifice form the closing list. Keep all six categories and their conjunctions rather than collapsing the middle ritual designations into a single term.

The commands are associated with Mount Sinai and the day Israel was told to bring gifts in the Sinai wilderness. Preserve both geographical phrases and the Lord-before-whom wording without inventing a second command occasion.
